query: Consider the following context: The recent perspective of multiprincipal element alloys (MPEAs), also known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs), has emerged as a very promising area for material design. Additive manufacturing (AM) strategies have also been noted to provide additional strength to HEA systems. In the selected dual-nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA system, an additional strength of approximately 300–400 MPa was achieved by adopting an additive manufacturing route as compared to its cast and wrought counterparts. However, the challenge of oxidation degradation always imposes a severe limitation for high-temperature applications in gas turbines, power plants, and aerospace components. Hence, ensuring material sustainability, longevity, and integrity for high-temperature applications inevitably requires the exploration of the oxidation behavior of alloys. In that context, which method can be used for elucidating the mechanistic aspects and elemental redistribution of nanoprecipitates on oxidation behavior, and why?

generation.hypothesis: In the AM‐processed dual‐nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA, high‐temperature oxidation causes selective segregation of oxidation‐active elements (notably Al and Ti) to the nanoprecipitate/matrix interfaces, which facilitates the formation of a protective oxide scale that enhances high-temperature oxidation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Dual‐nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA produced by additive manufacturing with a refined distribution of nanoprecipitates compared to cast or wrought samples.
generation.intervention: Expose the HEA to controlled high-temperature oxidation conditions (e.g., 800–1000°C in an oxidizing atmosphere) for a defined period.
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidation in a controlled atmosphere that mimics service environments such as gas turbines and aerospace applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The nanoprecipitates and their interfaces with the surrounding matrix.
generation.mechanism: Elevated temperatures induce oxidation of Al and Ti within the nanoprecipitates. This oxidation leads to preferential elemental segregation at the interfaces, promoting the formation of a finely distributed, protective oxide scale. This compositional redistribution should reduce oxidation rate by acting as a barrier to further oxygen penetration.
generation.predicted_outcome: Atom Probe Tomography (APT) analysis will reveal a significant enrichment of Al and Ti at the nanoprecipitate/matrix interfaces in oxidized samples, correlating with the presence of a continuous or graded protective oxide layer. This effect is expected to translate into improved oxidation resistance compared to the unoxidized state.
generation.baseline: The as-fabricated AM HEA state prior to oxidation, with a relatively homogeneous elemental distribution across the nanoprecipitates and matrix, and without an established oxide scale.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is specific to the dual‐nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA processed by additive manufacturing under laboratory-controlled high-temperature oxidation conditions and may not directly apply to other HEA compositions or processing routes.
generation.uncertainty: The precise extent of elemental segregation and its quantitative impact on oxidation resistance remain to be determined. Additionally, contributions from other minor elements or secondary phase transformations are not fully characterized.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of dual‐nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA samples – one as the baseline (unoxidized) and another exposed to high-temperature oxidation (800–1000°C in air) for a predetermined time. Perform Atom Probe Tomography (APT) to generate three-dimensional compositional maps focusing on the nanoprecipitate/matrix interfaces, and supplement the analysis with TEM to characterize oxide scale formation and thickness.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the APT analysis does not show a statistically significant enrichment of Al and Ti at the nanoprecipitate interfaces in the oxidized samples compared to the baseline, or if no meaningful correlation is found between such segregation and enhanced oxide scale quality (as evidenced by TEM and weight gain data), then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) first appeared in public view in 2010 [ [1] ]. Thereafter, they aroused great concern from researchers at home and abroad. Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. The research shows that adding the proper amount of Al, Cr, and Si elements into the refractory high-entropy alloy can form a dense oxidation film on the surface of the alloy in a high-temperature environment, thus improving the high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] ]. This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. frame.system: The dual‐nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high‐entropy alloy (HEA) produced via additive manufacturing (AM), which has enhanced strength over its cast and wrought forms.
frame.goal: To elucidate the mechanistic aspects and elemental redistribution of nanoprecipitates during oxidation, thereby understanding how these microstructural features affect high-temperature performance.
frame.limitation: Oxidation degradation limits the alloy's use in high-temperature applications like gas turbines, power plants, and aerospace components.
constraints: High-temperature service environments (e.g., gas turbines, power plants, aerospace)
Need to maintain material sustainability, longevity, and integrity in oxidation conditions
prior_attempts: Cast and wrought processing routes, which did not achieve the enhanced strength and possibly provided less control over nanoprecipitate distribution and oxidation behavior compared to AM.
frame.understanding: Using a technique with near-atomic spatial resolution to capture 3D elemental distributions and interface characteristics of nanoprecipitates under oxidation conditions is essential.
frame.recommended_method: Atom Probe Tomography (APT) is the method of choice. It provides three-dimensional compositional mapping at near-atomic resolution, which is critical for elucidating the detailed elemental redistribution and interfacial characteristics of the nanoprecipitates. This level of insight is necessary to understand the mechanisms by which oxidation affects the nanoprecipitate distribution and, ultimately, the high-temperature performance of the alloy.

decision.trend: Earlier studies on high-entropy alloys have first focused on improving strength and oxidation resistance using conventional processing (cast, wrought, or friction-processed) and then utilizing additive manufacturing to refine microstructures and nanoprecipitate distributions. Methods like SEM, TEM, XRD and even limited APT have been applied to relate oxide scale formation to grain refinement and phase transformation but have left the atomic-scale mechanisms, including the precise elemental redistribution at nanoprecipitate/matrix interfaces during oxidation, underexplored.
decision.unsolved: A critical gap remains in directly visualizing and quantifying the near‐atomic compositional evolution and interfacial characteristics of nanoprecipitates during high-temperature oxidation. This unresolved mechanistic detail hampers deeper understanding of how nanoprecipitate behavior influences oxidation resistance in AM-processed HEAs.
decision.lever: Atom Probe Tomography (APT) with 3D compositional mapping
decision.why: APT offers near-atomic spatial resolution and three-dimensional elemental mapping, directly addressing the need to elucidate mechanistic aspects of elemental redistribution in nanoprecipitates during oxidation. This approach follows naturally from prior work that highlighted the role of nanoprecipitates in strengthening while leaving their oxidation behavior at the atomic level insufficiently understood.
